DEFALCATIONS

label: text
text:
一

一

label: text
text: Chan Lam, a shroff in the local Treasury, again came before the police court this morning on charges of embezzlement of sums paid in as rates.

label: text
text: Mr. J. M. Hall, who represented defendant, said that his client admitted taking over $7,000.

label: text
text: Mr. T. M. Hazlerigg, for the Crown, said that $6,500 had actually been traced but it was thought that the total amount would be something like $7,400.

label: text
text: Mr. Hazlerigg said that the defendant had not given assistance in tracing the defalcations. It was, of course, difficult to ask defendant to sit down and write out a complete list of all the money mislaid as it concerned some sixty properties. "Defendant's work, up to the time of the misappropriations, had been satisfactory.

label: text
text: Mr. Hall, on behalf of defendant, pointed out to Mr. R. E. Lindsell, the Magistrate, that defendant had a large family to support. He had been in the Government service for eight or nine years. He would point out that the defendant had made no attempt to run away.

label: text
text: In reply to a question from the Magistrate, Mr. Hazlerigg said that there was little hope of obtaining reparation.

label: text
text: His Worship imposed sentences, on three of the four counts, amounting to nine months' imprisonment, and on the fourth charge a sentence of five months, the latter to run concurrently. The last charge concerned fraudulent application of a cheque for $2,045.89 made payable to the Government.

label: paragraph_title
text: CHARGES AGAINST THREE CHINESE.

label: paragraph_title
text: TEA-HOUSE ARRESTS

label: text
text: Mr. R. E. Lindsell and Major C. Willson sat together at the Central Magistracy this forenoon to deal with a case in which three Chinese were charged with the possession of implements such as are used in armed robberies. The articles which they were alleged to have been in possession were two daggers, a knife, a pointed file, two rolls of cotton waste done up in the form of gags and two rolls of wire.

label: text
text: Det.-Sub-Inspector "Lane gave evidence of a raid which he carried out on a ten-house at Sai Wan Ho (in the Shaukiwan district) on June 19 when he arrested the three defendants, another man who was seated with them at a table making his escape by the back door. He said that the first defendant dropped something from his girdle when he had him covered with his revolver. This was found to be a pointed file. One dagger was found where the man had his left foot. Another man on being searched had a knife and two gags, while the third had the other dagger and the wire.

label: text
text: There being a number of other witnesses, the case is proceeding.

label: doc_title
text: POWERS' COLD FEET.

label: doc_title
text:
REFUSE TO  $ \underline{\text{INTERVENE}} $ IN CHINA.
DR. SUN YAT-SEN'S DEATHBED VISION.

label: text
text: Leader's Sugg estion of 5-Year Foreign Garrisons.

label: text
text: The late Dr. Sun Yat-sen has been described by his soundest critics as a dreamer and a visionary. He has been accused of extending the first overtures to Russia and he is blamed for being responsible for the foothold Communism has gained in China, or strictly, in Canton.

label: text
text: But history has yet to record his proposals to the Treaty Powers, through the United States and Great Britain, whereby he wanted foreign intervention—armed if needs be—to evolve order out of chaos in China, with non-Chinese garrisons in the capitals and a complete form of government—for a stated period. How this did not come to pass because—to use our correspondent's own words—the Powers got "cold feet," is related in the article below.

label: text
text: In June, 1922, Dr. Sun was ousted from Canton by a subordinate of General Chan Kwingming. During his absence, documents were discovered showing the part that he took in the steps to establish an understanding with Moscow.

label: text
text: Subsequently, General Chan's regime terminated and Dr. Sun returned on the strength of his Yunnanese and Kwangsi mercenaries. After being in power again for another period, he went North to Peking, where he died. The Kuomintang commission of government began at Canton and, in view of recent events, most people are familiar with conditions to-day.

label: paragraph_title
text: SUN'S DESPAIR.

label: paragraph_title
text: First of Two Proposals

label: text
text: [From Our Own Correspondent.]

label: paragraph_title
text: Canton, July 4.

label: text
text: Twice before he died, Dr. Sun Yat-sen, China's great revolutionary leader, despaired of bringing order out of chaos in China and made secret proposals to the Treaty Powers, through the United States and Great Britain for active intervention.

label: text
text: The first proposal was made in 1923 on the occasion of the visit to Canton of Mr. Jacob Gould Schurman, U.S. Minister to Peking. Sun Yat-sen at that time said frankly to the American Minister that there was no man and no faction or party in China that had a chance of bringing peace to the troubled country. He sounded the Powers, through the American Minister, as to their willingness to agree to joint intervention, but the proposal was coldly received.

label: text
text: This is vouched for by reverations just made here by some of his disciples.

label: text
text: Again, in Peking, shortly before his death in March, 1925, Dr. Suh Yat-sen proposed active intervention. He was a dying man and he knew it. In the interval since his first proposal he had asked the Treaty Powers to send commissions and advisory boards to China to aid in the establishment of a stable government. That proposal, too, had been rejected. Meanwhile, in desperation, he had turned to Russia for money and advisers, and he had seen Communism gain a foothold in China as a result.

label: paragraph_title
text: Second Scheme Rejected.

label: paragraph_title
text: BOWLS SURPRISE.

label: text
text: REVENUE OFFICERS BEAT POLICE

label: paragraph_title
text: DEPT. CHAMPIONSHIP?

label: text
text: An inter-Departmental bowls competition may be started as the result of a match yesterday.

label: text
text: With only 13 men to pick from, the European Revenue officers got up a rink of four men and beat the Police, at the P.R.O., by 23 shots to 12. The sides were:—

label: text
text: Revenue Officers: Knight, Trengove, Beattie and Tallon (skip). Police: Fender, Condon, Dick and Sword (skip). The winners got the customary spoons.

label: text
text: It is stated that an anonymous donor will present a challenge cup with replicas, for the winning team and the following will be asked to compete: Police, Revenue Officers, Warders, Sanitary Department, P.W.D. The sponsors hope to put things through this season.

label: text
text: In Peking, realising that he had not long to live, he proposed to the American Minister a definite plan. The Treaty Powers, under American and British leadership, should come into China and garrison the provincial capitals. They should take over the government, send out experts, administrators and commissions of all kinds, and govern China in an orderly fashion for five years, inculcating ideals of order; honesty and efficiency.

label: paragraph_title
text: Not Without Bloodshed.

label: text
text: He proposed an iron-clad agreement that at the end of the five-year period the powers should begin gradual withdrawal, to be completed within a specified time, and that the government should then be turned over to responsible Chinese officials.

label: text
text: The Powers demurred. They declared that though they would be willing thus to aid the Chinese people, they feared the plan could not be carried out without blood-shed.

label: text
text: Dr. Sun Yat-sen countered with the proposal that he would be glad to issue a formal proclamation inviting such intervention. He pledged himself to use what remained to him of his life in propaganda work that would induce the Chinese people to accept the plan gladly. He believed that his personal following was sufficient to accomplish his purpose; and that there would be enough reasoning and unselfish Chinese among those who were not his followers, who would see that the plan was feasible and would help to promote

label: paragraph_title
text: Powers' Feelings.

label: text
text: But the Great Powers, to put it bluntly, "got cold feet." They remembered the utter failure of their after-the-war attempt at establishing a stable government in Siberia. Possibly each distrusted the other. At any rate, Dr. Sun's proposals were all rejected, and he died a heart-broken and disillusioned man, seeing his country torn between factional jealousies, and with Russians having an ominously firm foothold in Canton and the South.

label: text
text: To-day the followers of Dr. Sun Yat-sen have no knowledge of these proposals. They do not know of the despair of his latter days. They do not regard with friendliness the Powers that their great leader invited twice into China.

Every Monday, morning, the week's work is begun with a ritual in his honour. Whether it be in a primary school or a university, a government office, a military station, or aboard ship, reverence is paid to Dr. Sun.

label: text
text: All those present stand bareheaded, and then slowly bow three times toward his photograph, which graces the main wall of every room. Then Dr. Sun's last will and testament, a political document, is read. After this the people stand in silence for three minutes of contemplation of his principles.

label: paragraph_title
text: Secret Not Yet Revealed.

label: text
text: There is much pathos in these reverential ceremonies. From the framed photograph on the wall the tired eyes look out from a careworn face. If they could see, those eyes would look upon a multitude that has no knowledge of their dead leader's last hopes and secret appeal for intervention. They would look upon the multitude of people led astray and deceived into bitter hostility against the very nations that Dr. Sun believed could become China's best friends, the nations with whom, he believed, rested China's sole hope.

label: text
text: Sun Yat-sen had vision. He has been dead for fifteen months, and to-day the condition of China is even more chaotic than it was when, in desperation, he asked for intervention. Of the eighteen enormous provinces in China not more than five owe allegiance to any one government.

label: paragraph_title
text: Did Opportunity Slip?

label: text
text: Peking, which continues to hold the recognition of the Treaty Powers, is a shadow of power passing from the control of one War Lord to another, and now without a properly constituted governmental head with whom the Powers can treat.

label: text
text: China 'has known fifteen months of bloodshed and pillage since Dr. Sun died, and the end is not yet in sight. He proposed the only chance for bloodless intervention that has ever been thought out.

label: text
text: But the Father of, the Revolution is dead, and the millions whom he might have led to "accept" intervention peacefully, the millions who now do reverence to his picture every Monday morning, have been taught to hate the nations their dead leader believed could save China.

text: Thirteen persons were killed 50 injured through the collapse of a roof in the village of Woltersdorf, near Berlin.
